Good afternoon. I call to order the second meeting of the Sixth Committee for the 81st session of the General Assembly. Distinguished delegates, this afternoon the Sixth Committee will continue with its debate on agenda item 112, measures to eliminate international terrorism. The report of the Secretary General on the item is contained in document A/81/218 and Corr. 1, which is available on the website of the Sixth Committee. The first speaker on the list for this afternoon is the distinguished representative of the United Kingdom. You have the floor.

Thank you, Chair. The United Kingdom reaffirms its commitment to preventing and countering terrorism in all its forms and manifestations. Last month, we stood with the United States and countries across the world to commemorate 25 years since the appalling terrorist attacks of 9/11. And as we approach the third anniversary of Hamas's horrific terrorist attacks of 7th of October, we remember all those killed and affected by terrorism. Terrorist groups continue to adapt, exploit instability and operate across borders. Daesh, al-Qaeda and their affiliates remain a threat in many regions, while emerging technologies, online platforms and new methods of financing are creating new opportunities for terrorists to radicalise, recruit and organise. Our response must evolve accordingly. No country can address these challenges alone. International cooperation remains essential to strengthening our collective understanding of the threat, disrupting terrorist networks, and supporting those most affected by terrorism. The United Kingdom values the contribution of the United Nations counter-terrorism architecture in these efforts. The ISIL, Daesh, and Al-Qaeda Sanctions Committee's analytical support and sanctions monitoring team continues to provide authoritative analysis of the evolving threat landscape. CTED and UNOCT support Member States in strengthening implementation and building capacity across the international system. Effective counter-terrorism depends on respect for human rights, the rule of law and international law more widely. In doing so, we strengthen the legitimacy and effectiveness of our response and deny terrorists a powerful tool for recruitment and radicalization. The UK remains committed to ensuring that gender equality and the women, peace and security agenda remain central to international counter-terrorism efforts. We also recognise the important role that victims and survivors, women and young people can play in building resilience against violent extremism and strengthening prevention efforts. Earlier this year, member states adopted the ninth review of the United Nations Global Counter-Terrorism Strategy, marking 20 years since the strategy's first adoption. The United Kingdom continues to regard the strategy as the cornerstone of our collective international efforts to prevent and counter terrorism. While we regret that consensus could not be achieved, we remain firmly committed to the strategy's objectives and principles. In closing, the UK remains committed to working with all member states through the United Nations to strengthen international cooperation and counter terrorism in all its forms and manifestations. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of the United Kingdom for his statement. And I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of the State of Palestine.

Thank you, Madam Chair. And we are happy to see you up there. We congratulate you and assure you of Palestine's full cooperation. We align ourselves with the statement made by the OIC. The State of Palestine unequivocally condemns and rejects terrorism in all its forms and manifestations, wherever, by whomever, and against whomsoever committed. We reiterate that terrorism cannot and should not be associated with any religion, race, faith, culture, ethnicity, or society. Politicization of the fight against terrorism serves only the interests and aspirations of terrorists and promotes polarization, hatred, discrimination, xenophobia, and hostility. We have long emphasized the need for a multilateral, cooperative, and non-discriminatory approach to tackling terrorism, including by finalizing the draft comprehensive convention on international terrorism, and the necessity to uphold the right to self-determination of peoples, notably of those struggling to realize their legitimate rights under colonial or alien domination and foreign occupation, as enshrined in international law. Madam Chair, terrorism in its essence is a denial of human rights and the violation of basic dignity and security. For decades, the Palestinian people have endured the denial of our existence and of our rights, including the right to life, to self-determination, to security, to safety, to freedom and independence, the denial of our belonging to our land, our rights as human beings and as a people. Israel has used terrorism to advance its settler colonial project and entrench its illegal presence in Palestine. The methods have changed from sexual violence, rape, starvation, famine, torture, murder, reaching its most extreme genocide. But the underlying logic remained the same. Dispossess the Palestinian people, annex their land, uproot them and eliminate Palestinian life. In the West Bank, backed and supported by every Israeli institution, political echelon, judicial system, the army and Israeli officials, terrorism is part of a comprehensive, coordinated system used as a calculated, targeted tool to execute colonialist aspirations and settlement enterprise, fueled by a racist and religious ideology of superiority. This terrorism is not new. It is decades-long process of ethnic cleansing. but since 2023 it has accelerated. The UN documented over 6,100 settler terrorist attacks against the Palestinian people, an average of four to five terrorist attacks daily, sanctioned, advanced, facilitated, funded, protected, and supported by the state. with the aim to displace the Palestinian people, steal their land, carry out ethnic cleansing, erase the existence of a whole indigenous people, destroy and appropriate their culture and history, and impose a manufactured settlement enterprise on their land. The equation is clear. Each Palestinian displaced by terror is replaced by settlers through terror. Each Palestinian community demolished is replaced by settlements. The settlers, under the protection of the state, terrorize the people to displace them. The state, with the help of its settlers, expands its settlement enterprise. Simultaneously, in the Gaza Strip, Israel continues to erase Palestinian life and conditions of life through terrorism, mass killing, destruction, displacement, starvation, and attacks on entire life-sustaining systems. Since the announcement of the ceasefire a year ago, Israel has killed over 1,300 people, including over 350 children. 2.3 million people, half of whom are children, are besieged, barely surviving in a constant atmosphere of terror, death and destruction, starved and constantly bombed. This is the gravest form of terrorism. An entire defenseless population is marked for destruction with no end in sight. An entire people are killed, displaced, assaulted, and terrorized daily, killed in bombardments or in attacks by settlers and occupation forces, killed as they sleep, as they tend to their groves, as they head to schools, as they sit in their homes, as they pray in their churches and mosques, killed as if their lives never matter, as if they were expendable. A mass collective punishment unseen in our world in this century. Confronting this terrorism means holding Israel accountable, not simply the individual settlers and groups. The international community must provide the Palestinian people with international protection and must compel Israel to end its illegal occupation and dismantle its settlement enterprise and apartheid regime. Each day under Israel's oppression is a day of terror. Israel not only uses terrorism to advance its colonial project, it has weaponized the discourse of counterterrorism and turned it into counter-rights, counter-life, counter-United Nations, counter-humanity discourse to both serve its political interests over the common good and to justify committing mass atrocities, corroding the integrity and efficacy of the global legal order, an order which it is actively trying to destroy. We reject the politicization of the right against terrorism, and we reiterate that the global fight against terrorism is inherently about equality and non-discrimination. It is about justice and fairness. It is about self-determination and freedom. It is about the rule of law and the global order. The State of Palestine reiterates that only those who adhere to their obligations under international law can truly call themselves equal partners in our global fight against terrorism. The law is what distinguishes us from the terrorists. Law is what distinguishes peace-loving states from rogue states and is intrinsic to the United Nations counterterrorism architecture. Finally, we condemn all attacks against civilians anywhere in the world, whether Palestinian or Israeli, and we insist that international law is our reference. We commit ourselves to the United Nations Charter, its purpose and principles, to the ICJ and to the UN resolutions, and to the sanctity of human life, all human lives. And we reject the spirit of fear and the use of indiscriminate violence to achieve political aims. Such acts are antithetical to the values of humanity and the foundational principles of this organization. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Palestine for her statement, and I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Portugal.

Thank you, Madam Chair, and congratulations for your election. It's a pleasure to see you and your country presiding the Sixth Committee. Portugal aligns itself with the statement delivered by the European Union and its member states and would like to add the following in its national capacity. Terrorism remains a serious threat to international peace and security. It exploits conflict, governance, gaps, inequality, mistrust, and digital openness. No state is immune. For Portugal, an Atlantic nation with ties across Europe, Africa, and Latin America, counterterrorism is inseparable from maritime security, border management and international cooperation. We approach counter-terrorism as an international justice and prevention issue. Our national counter-terrorism strategy is built on four axes: prevent, protect, pursue and respond. And the prevention we prioritize countering hate speech and disinformation only because they fuel radicalization. We have ratified all UN counterterrorism instruments. We insist that counterterror measures must never serve as a pretext for human rights violations or be directed against civil society. Prevention requires addressing conditions conducive to terrorism. We have invested in community level programs, reintegration and support for vulnerable youth. We also support the full, equal and meaningful participation of women and youth and the central role of victims and survivors. Portugal is deeply committed to the UN Global Counter-Terrorism Strategy. We support efforts to strengthening accountability and transparency of UN counter-terrorism entities and fair and clear procedure for listing and delisting. And we maintain a close cooperation with the UN Office of Counterterrorism, who's have as recently on a working visit to Lisbon. Madam Chair, Portugal engagements is also regional within the community of Portuguese speaking countries, the CPLP. We cooperate very closely with Lusophone partners in Africa as well as Timor-Leste. We provide training in criminal investigation, cybercrime, explosive ordnance disposal, and public order with all of them. These are sustained partnerships, not one-off gesture. In Mozambique, Portugal is strongly engaged. The instability in the north of Mozambique in Cabo Delgado has displaced tens of thousands, mostly women, the elderly, and persons with disabilities. Since 2021, My country has led a defence cooperation project training Mozambican forces in counter-terrorism, including quick reaction forces, with training in protection of civilians, international humanitarian law and human rights. We are the main contributor to the European Union Military Assistance Mission in Mozambique and have held its force commander since the EU's engagement began in 2021. We have trained and equipped 11 quick reaction forces. and we will continue to do so, and we support the continuation of the EU engagement in Mozambique. Effective counter-terrorism cannot be delivered in isolation from peacebuilding, development and governance. We do support integrated strategies that combine security, development and human rights, and we emphasize that poverty, exclusion and lack of opportunity are catalysts for recruitment by armed groups. Portugal shares the EU concern about emerging technologies. Terrorist groups exploit digital platforms, artificial intelligence, satellite communications and drones. We support a multi-stakeholder approach with the private sector, civil society and academia to ensure responsible use of technology in line with human rights. Finally, In concluding, Portugal strongly supports revitalized negotiations on the Comprehensive Convention on International Terrorism. The recent protocol amending the Council of European Convention on the Prevention of Terrorism shows that shared legal definitions are possible while safeguarding human rights. We stand ready to engage constructively, including on the question of a high-level conference. and we remain steadfast in multilateralism. We will continue to work with all partners to strengthen collective security, uphold the rule of law, and protect human dignity. Terrorism exploits fragility and division. Our response must be firm, but always faithful to the values that define us. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Portugal for the statement. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Gambia.

Chair, at the outset, I would like to congratulate you and esteemed members of the Bureau on your election to the leadership of this important committee, and assure you of the cooperation and full support of my delegation during this 81st session. We thank the Secretary-General for the report contained in document A/81/218, and have duly taken note of the content stipulated therein. My delegation aligns with the statement delivered on behalf of the OIC, as well as the statement delivered on behalf of the African Group, and we wish to make the following remarks in our national capacity. The Gambia renews its unwavering commitment to strengthening international cooperation in the fight against the scourge of terrorism. We believe that there cannot be any justifiable reasons for the atrocities committed by acts of terrorism, regardless of the motivation, where and whomsoever committed it. It is in this context that The Gambia unequivocally condemns all acts of terrorism and reaffirms its commitment to supporting counterterrorism efforts at every level of national and global governance. Terrorism is not only a regional or continental issue, but an international problem that poses a clear and present danger to global peace and security, and serves as an affront to the values espoused in the UN Charter. This requires us to confront the threats posed by terrorism and garner the requisite policies and resources to confront common challenges. It is well too known that acts of terrorists operate without respect for territorial borders. And as a result, the international community must engage in meaningful consultations by sharing best practices on winning the threats to stem the tide of violent extremists, which inexorably erodes peace and security. To achieve this objective also requires us to gather the root causes of radicalization and violent extremism to materialize our responsibility to protect the most vulnerable communities against the threats of terrorism. Chair, The Gambia believes that any measures taken to counter terrorism must adhere strictly with human rights principles and obligations espoused on the international humanitarian law and international refugee law, as these are foundational ethos of ensuring that sustainable counterterrorism measures are imbued with legitimacy and effectiveness. Accordingly, we also need to strengthen early warning mechanisms, support regional initiatives to control small and light weapons circulation, monitor crisis situations, and enhance preventive diplomacy. In its briefing last year at the UN Security Council on the topic called African-led and development-focused counterterrorism initiatives under the chairship of Algeria, the ECOWAS detailed out the measures galvanized to respond to the growing challenges of terrorism in the West African region. This includes the adoption of the ECOWAS plan of action for the eradication of terrorism, the activation of the ECOWAS Standby Force, and the introduction of kinetic means in intervention strategies. Considering the constructive efforts deployed by ECOWAS, we continue to call for enhanced international support of Africa's initiatives by integrating social economic development into counterterrorism approaches. To avoid the impending consequence of terrorist activities, we must put the onus on tackling poverty and inequality, strengthening state institutions and civil society as a high priority to build resilient communities and societies. The preservation of international peace and security demands that we act swiftly and proactively. Chair, as we mark the 20th anniversary of the ninth review of the United Nations Global Counterterrorism Strategy, we welcome the adoption of the resolution approved this year and all member states of the United Nations to take proactive measures, pursuant to international law, to address all drivers of terrorism and violent extremism. While we regret that the ninth review had its challenges, we continue to call for the balanced implementation of the four pillars of the strategy, ensuring that due priority is given to counterterrorism, determinately rooted in implementation of the strategy. The Gambia emphasizes that countering the criminal misuse of information and communication technologies requires stronger international cooperation to establish clear rules, governance frameworks, guidelines, and practical tools to ensure these technologies are not used by terrorists to exploit sophisticated technologies across borders, creating complex risk to international peace and security. We recall relevant Security Council resolutions on women, peace, and security, recognizing women's vital role in preventing acts of terrorism. and condemn terrorist groups' systematic targeting of women and girls. The Gambia supports genuine efforts to ensure women's full, equal, meaningful participation and leadership in preventing and countering terrorism in partnership with relevant stakeholders, and we welcome the acknowledgement of women's role as espoused in the resolution adopted in June. Chair, despite regional and international commitments to monitor the financing of terrorism, it is unfortunate that the implementation of the commitments has proven difficult. Accordingly, The Gambia continues to call for more proactive measures to strengthen accountability for illicit financing flows to suppress the financing of terrorism. We urge continued financial, logistical, and operational support to regional bodies and member states to increase their capabilities in preventing the financing of terrorism. Addressing this is crucial to prevent future terrorist attacks. Chair, The Gambia reiterates its principal stance against the recruitment and use of children by terrorist organizations. This practice is not only a moral and legal atrocity, it undermines our collective vision of peace, prosperity, and sustainable development. And we continue to call on the international community to strengthen monitoring and accountability mechanisms to ensure that perpetrators of child recruitment and other grave violations are brought to justice. We support member states in implementing the Safe Schools Declaration and other relevant frameworks to uphold the rights and protection of children. Finally, the Gambia also joins the growing calls for the promulgation of a comprehensive convention on international terrorism and to convene a high-level meeting in this regard under the leadership of the United Nations. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Gambia for the statement. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of the Islamic Republic of Iran on behalf of a group.

Thank you, Madam Chair. I have the honor to deliver this statement on behalf of a like-minded group comprising Belarus, Burundi, China, Cuba, the Democratic Republic of -- People's Republic of Korea, Equatorial Guinea, Eritrea, the Lao People's Democratic Republic, Mali, Nicaragua, the Niger, the Russian Federation, the State of Palestine, Uganda, and Zimbabwe, and including my own country, the Islamic Republic of Iran. Madam Chair, terrorist acts endanger human lives, threaten the territorial integrity and security of states, and undermine regional and international peace, security, and stability. As stipulated in the Declaration on Measures to Eliminate International Terrorism, I quote, "Acts, methods, and practices of terrorism constitute a grave violation of the purposes and principles of the United Nations," end of quote. As a like-minded group, we reaffirm our categorical rejection and unequivocal condemnation of terrorism in all its forms and manifestations, and of all acts of terrorism, regardless of their motivation, wherever, whenever, and by whomsoever committed. We wish to underline that all acts, methods, and practices of terrorism are criminal and unjustifiable. The full and good faith implementation by all the states of their obligations in preventing and combating terrorism remains a crucial element and the path to achieve a world free of terrorism. We recall in this regard duties of every state with respect to combating international terrorism, including the duty to refrain from organizing, instigating, assisting, participating in, financing, facilitating, encouraging, or otherwise tolerating terrorist acts. We further recall the duty of every state to refrain from organizing, assisting, fomenting, financing, inciting, or tolerating terrorist activities directed against sovereign states, including against members of our group, as reflected in the Declaration on the Principles of International Law and the Declaration on Measures to Eliminate International Terrorism, respectively contained in General Assembly resolution 2625 and resolution 49/60. We stress that terrorism shall in no way be equated with the legitimate struggle of peoples under colonial or alien domination and foreign occupation to self-determination and national liberation. We further reaffirm that terrorism cannot and should not be associated with any religion, nationality, civilization, or ethnic group. Terrorism cannot be defeated by military force, law enforcement measures, and intelligence operations alone. As such, we cannot overemphasize the importance of comprehensively addressing its root causes in order to effectively overcome conditions that may provide breeding grounds for the promotion of criminal agendas based on extremism and racism, including supremacism and neo-Nazism, and which seek to exploit divisions, inflame tensions, and foster the commission of terrorist acts. We express our concerns at the use of digital platforms and other information and communication technologies to incite, facilitate, and finance terrorist acts as well as to advance destabilizing agendas against sovereign states, and also in pursuit of policies and practices aimed at no colonial domination, including through modern no colonial practices. In this regard, we underline the need for strengthening and promoting cooperation of global digital platforms with competent law enforcement authorities of the states in which they operate as a crucial element in preventing and combating terrorism and counter-terrorist narratives and preventing the use of such platforms for terrorist purposes. Madam Chair, fighting terrorism still faces serious challenges that undermine genuine efforts in countering this discourse. These include gross violations of the fundamental principles of international law, including by imposing unilateral coercive measures, as well as double standards, selectivity, and politicization of the fight against terrorism. In this regard, we categorically reject the entrenched policy and practice of creating, in the first place, lists accusing other states or their constitutionally established armed forces of terrorism. A corollary of the principle of par in parium, non abe imperium, is that the states, as equals, may not initiate to exert such unacceptable and unlawful measures against each other. Such measures constitute a flagrant violation of the fundamental principles of international law, in particular sovereign equality and non-intervention, are also in contravention of both the purposes and principles of the Charter of the UN, while only serving the malign interests of terrorist groups and running counter to relevant obligations assumed by states in the fight against terrorism. In this regard, we wish to refer in particular to the false accusations leveled against Cuba and its unjustified inclusion in the illegal and unnatural list of countries falsely accused of sponsoring terrorism, fabricated by the United States. which has significantly reinforced the negative effects of the criminal and illegal economic, commercial, and financial blockade imposed against the Cuban people, including by creating enormous difficulties in carrying out financial and commercial operations and causing serious damages to substances and integrity of Cuban population. In this context, we emphasize the need to abolish such lists and in particular call for the immediate removal of Cuba from that arbitrary and unilateral list, which we firmly reject in its entirety. Madam Chair, it would be irresponsible from us to address this agenda item without referring to the ongoing situation in the Middle East. We express our most serious concerns at the continued unwillingness of Israel to carry out obligations contained in the Charter of the United Nations, as well as the attempts of Israel, the occupying power, to ignite and explode the Middle East region as a whole, as demonstrated, among others, by its reiterated gross violations of international law. including through its provocations and violations against the sovereignty and territorial integrity of countries in the region, which demonstrate its intent to escalate tensions on the ground. We condemn the Israeli deliberate use of starvation and forcible displacement of millions of Palestinian people. We wish to reiterate our condemnation in the strongest possible terms of the unprovoked and permeated heinous attacks of the United States and Israel against the Islamic Republic of Iran, including since February 2026, which killed thousands of civilians, especially 168 elementary school children and teachers in a school in Minab City, an aggression that all of us have categorically denounced in the strongest possible terms, including as reflected in the relevant document submitted before the United Nations. To conclude, Madam Chair, we wish to reaffirm the leading role and primary responsibility of States in prevention and countering terrorism. We underline the importance of finalizing the process towards the conclusion of the comprehensive convention on international terrorism, while highlighting the need for a balanced approach within the UN system in relation to the implementation of the United Nations Global Counter-Terrorism Strategy, as reaffirmed in its ninth review adopted earlier this year. I thank you.
Thank the distinguished representative of Iran for the statement. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Malaysia.

Thank you, Madam Chair. Malaysia aligns itself with the statement presented by the Non-Aligned Movement, OIC and ASEAN. Additionally, we would like to take this opportunity to deliver a statement in our national capacity. Malaysia remains resolute in its rejection of terrorism in all forms and manifestations. No cause or objective can justify attacks against civilians or other acts that constitute terrorism. Malaysia stresses that the fight against terrorism requires sustained cooperation among states, supported by effective law enforcement, information sharing, and measures to prevent the financing and facilitation of terrorism activities. Malaysia continues to pursue a comprehensive approach to counterterrorism, including preventive efforts aimed at strengthening community resilience and addressing radicalization. In this regard, Malaysia has experienced through the Southeast Asia Regional Centre for Counterterrorism continues to contribute to regional capacity building, technical cooperation, and the sharing of practical expertise. Malaysia also places importance on regional cooperation. Our participation in ASEAN mechanisms, including the ASEAN Convention on Counter-Terrorism and the ASEAN Mutual Legal Assistance Treaty, supports closer cooperation in preventing and responding to terrorism and facilitates practical assistance between relevant authorities. Madam Chair, Malaysia welcomes the continuation of efforts in the Sixth Committee towards finalizing the draft Comprehensive Convention on International Terrorism. Malaysia observes that the significant divergence in the position of Member States persists following the deliberations of the previous session. In this regard, Malaysia supports the establishment of a working group at the 81st session as envisaged in the General Assembly resolution 80/171 and encourage continued constructive engagement to achieving consensus on the outstanding issues. The establishment of a working group provides an important opportunity to carry this work forward. Malaysia also remains steadfast in its support for convening a high-level conference under the auspices of the United Nations. Malaysia believes the initiatives can be advanced in tandem with ongoing efforts regarding the CCIT. Crucially, the convening of the conference should not be contingent upon the conclusion of the CCIT, as it holds distinct values in fostering broader international dialogue and reinforcing our collective fight against terrorism. Malaysia further recognises that the threat of terrorism is being shaped by developments in technology, the misuse of artificial intelligence, virtual assets, and unmanned aircraft systems, as highlighted by Malaysia during the 9th review of the United Nations Global Counterterrorism Strategy in July 2026, demonstrates the need for international cooperation to keep pace with emerging methods of terrorist activity and financing. Malaysia remains committed to working with all Member States in strengthening the international response to terrorism. We believe that continued dialogue, practical cooperation, and respect for international law are essential to our common efforts to prevent and eliminate terrorism. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Malaysia for the statement, and I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of South Africa.

Thank you, Madam Chair. Madam Chair, like others, I wish to congratulate you and my fellow Bureau members on your election. Please be assured of my delegation's support. South Africa aligns with the statements delivered by Cameroon on behalf of the African Group and Iran on behalf of the Non-Aligned Movement. South Africa expresses gratitude to the Secretary-General for the report on measures to eliminate international terrorism, as contained in document A/81/218. Madam Chair, terrorism is a serious threat to international peace and security. South Africa condemns all acts of terrorism and violent extremism conducive to terrorism. The inducement of fear through violence has no place in today's world. Whilst it would appear that the number of deaths from terrorism has been decreasing over the last decade, terrorism continues to be a global threat. The underlying factors which contribute to terrorism show no signs of subsiding. Conflict, being the primary driver of terrorism, is on the rise. Whilst the numbers reported differ, they are in excess of 65 conflicts globally. These conflicts are occurring in almost every continent. The underlying reasons differ. In some regions, the primary driving factors are economic, and in others, isolation leading to radicalisation among the youth, is becoming increasingly prevalent. It is essential that the underlying reasons for such terrorism are confronted. Ultimately, it is critical to start addressing the socio-economic factors that contribute to fostering terrorism. Madam Chair, according to the 13th Annual Global Terrorism Index, the GTI, nearly 70% of all global terrorism deaths occurred in just five countries, majority being African countries. The region remains the global terrorism epicenter, and this disturbing occurrence exacerbates the vulnerabilities faced by Africans as victims of terrorism. The scourge of terrorism needs to be addressed without delay. Madam Chair, whilst addressing terrorism is of primary importance, South Africa also acknowledges the disturbing misuse of terrorism language, which is often directed towards legitimate organizations and humanitarian efforts. It is critical that in carrying out counter-terrorism actions, politicization and double standards are not applied. Crucially, the legitimate right of self-determination carried out in accordance with international law remains paramount and should never be labeled as terrorism. Similarly, organizations exercising and pursuing legitimate human rights and humanitarian efforts must never be cast as terrorists. Doing so risks undermining the credibility of true counterterrorism efforts. Madam Chair, methods of carrying out terrorism attacks as well as radicalization are also changing. The use of unmanned systems and new technologies, such as artificial intelligence, is growing a concern, and it is essential that the international community is ready to respond appropriately and not be caught on the back foot. Whilst the primary responsibility for combating terrorism lies on States to act in their individual capacities, it would be a mistake to ignore the instrumental role that international cooperation plays in addressing terrorism. In this regard, South Africa remains committed to developing a comprehensive, balanced and international response to terrorism, which encompasses a convention that will unequivocally condemn and combat terrorism, while fully respecting international law, especially human rights and humanitarian law. In conclusion, Madam Chair, South Africa wishes to register deep concern and its regret that the Ninth Global Counter-Terrorism Review Strategy has, due to rigid negotiation tactics based on red lines and lack of flexibility, yielded no positive outcome and was reduced to a mere technical rollover. In addition to this disappointing outcome, for the first time since the strategy's inception in 2006, the review failed to pass by consensus and was adopted through a recorded vote. If we are to win the fight against terrorism, we need to show a united front in international processes aimed at strengthening cooperation. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of South Africa for the statement. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Slovenia.

Thank you and congratulations, Madam Chair. Slovenia aligns itself with the statement delivered on behalf of the EU and its member states and would like to add the following remarks in our national capacity. At the outset, Slovenia welcomes the report of the Secretary-General contained in document A/81/281. Madam Chair, terrorism in all its forms and manifestations remains one of the most serious threats to international peace and security, human rights and sustainable development. There can be no justification for the deliberate targeting of civilians, regardless of motive. Slovenia remains fully committed to all four pillars of the UN Global Counter-Terrorism Strategy and to a comprehensive approach firmly anchored in the rule of law and respect for human rights. Madam Chair, nearly three decades after negotiations began, we regret that the draft Comprehensive Convention on International Terrorism has still not been finalized. Slovenia supports the continuation of the working group and calls on all delegations to engage constructively and bridge the remaining differences. A comprehensive, legally binding instrument would strengthen legal certainty and international cooperation, including extradition and mutual legal assistance. Its adoption would also send an important signal of the international community's unity in confronting terrorism. Madam Chair, this unity should not be taken for granted. we are concerned that the long-standing international consensus on counter-terrorism has increasingly come under strain. Fragmentation and politicization risk undermining two decades of collective efforts and normative progress. We therefore call on all Member States to safeguard this consensus. At the same time, effective counterterrorism and the protection of human rights are mutually reinforcing. All counterterrorism measures must comply with states' obligations under international law, in particular international human rights law, international humanitarian law, and international refugee law. We also remain committed to protecting the rights, needs, and dignity of victims of terrorism. Finally, Madam Chair, our policies must keep pace with an evolving threat. Online radicalization, particularly among young people, the misuse of AI, drones and crypto assets, links with organized crime and CBRN-related risks require stronger prevention, international cooperation and capacity building. Slovenia stands ready, nationally and through the collective work of the European Union, to contribute constructively to the finalization of the draft Comprehensive Convention and to a united, effective UN counter-terrorism architecture grounded in international law. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Slovenia for the statement, and I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Cameroon.

Madame la President, permettez-moi tout d'abord.

Chair, allow me at the outset to assure you of the full cooperation of my delegation with the Bureau of our Committee, which you are leading, and we congratulate you on that, Madam Chair. Cameroon lines itself for the statement that was delivered on behalf of the African Group and would like to share certain points in its national capacity. We note the report of the USG 81/218. And core agenda one on measures to eliminate international terrorism. We reaffirm our firm and unequivocal condemnation of all forms of terrorism, a phenomenon that my country continues, unfortunately, to suffer from in its northern region with the attacks of Boko Haram. Madam Chair, the ninth review of the global counterterrorism strategy of the UN reaffirmed the importance of a comprehensive, integrated, and balanced approach, focusing on the strategy's four pillars. This ought to lead to a more tangible, coherent, and adapted implementation that is tailored to national and regional realities. Recent developments demonstrate that terrorism remains a transnational threat that is evolving and multifaceted, which especially affects regions of Africa. The SG's report presents as part of the ninth review of the strategy, the persistence of the Boko Haram group in the Lake Chad Basin and the activities of groups affiliated with ISIS in various regions of the continent. This confirms the need for strengthened international cooperation based upon trust, solidarity, and respect for the principles of the UN Charter. Beyond disagreements that could exist between states on certain issues, it is important to maintain constructive dialogue on the legal and conceptual aspects that are still pending, especially those relating to the definition of terrorism and stigmatization of certain religions or their symbols. In this regard, CAMERON reaffirms its commitment to finalizing negotiations on the draft General Convention on International Terrorism. This instrument would contribute to consolidating the international legal framework, strengthening cooperation between states, and further promoting legal security in the prevention and punishment of terrorism. Madam Chair, the ninth review of the Global Counterterrorism Strategy reaffirms as well the importance of a comprehensive and preventive approach toward combating terrorism, which adds, in addition to security measures, actions to strengthen societal resilience and to prevent radicalization and recruitment processes, therefore promoting social cohesion. education, awareness-raising, and the involvement of communities, as well as the creation of prospects for young people, are important factors of prevention. Cameroon remains committed to promoting these approaches and believes that efforts made in these regards ought to be supported by strengthened international cooperation, greater exchanges of good practices, and assistance that is adapted to the priorities and realities of each state. The strategy underscores the importance of collective and coordinated mobilization of all actors involved. Madam Chair, another priority lies in the adaptation of our actions to new technologies. Terrorist groups are increasingly exploiting digital tools and emerging technologies for propaganda, recruitment, radicalization, financing, and for preparing attacks. Our response, therefore, ought to bolster national capacity when it comes to cybersecurity, border control, information sharing, and digital investigations, while ensuring that the usage of these technologies to combat terrorism is in strict accordance with international law. At the same time, The issue of financing terrorism remains something we must curb. We must strengthen financial intelligence mechanisms, as well as legal cooperation, mutual assistance, and exchange of information, including between African states and international and regional mechanisms. Madam Chair, atrocities committed by Boko Haram and other terrorist groups operating in the Sahel region and the Lake Chad Basin continue to constitute a major challenge to peace, security, and development in our states. Cameroon remains fully committed to regional international mechanisms that aim to strengthen counterterrorism cooperation. Madam Chair, 20 years after the adoption of the Global Counterterrorism Strategy, our collective responsibility is to ensure that its principles are translated into concrete outcomes on the ground. The persistent threat of terrorism means that we ought to bolster our unity, cooperation, and resolve, while ensuring that our responses continue to be in accordance with the UN Charter and international law. I thank the distinguished representative of Cameroon for the statement, and I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Morocco.

I thank the distinguished representative of Nigeria for his statement. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Guatemala.

Madam Chair. Guatemala congratulates you and the other members of the Bureau on your election, and we assure you of our support during this session. Terrorist acts run counter to the purposes and principles of the United Nations Charter and pose a grave threat to international peace and security, human rights, democratic stability and the development of nations. Madam Chair, just a few days ago, before the General Assembly, the Guatemalan Minister for Foreign Affairs noted that transnational organized crime is not merely a threat to public safety. It is a direct threat to democracy, the rule of law, and the ability of peoples to freely decide over their future. Criminal networks know no borders. Their networks spread through drugs trafficking, trafficking in persons, the illicit trafficking of weapons, smuggling, extortion, and money laundering. The routes, intermediaries, and financial circuits that maintain these networks are the very same that finance and facilitate acts of terrorism. These acts not only harm the population, they also weaken the state, preventing it from delivering on protecting people and guaranteeing the common good. Today, Guatemala is pleased to tell you that this bill has been enacted into our domestic law. Guatemala would like to highlight four specific areas of progress within the Act. Firstly, it expands the catalogue of entities covered by the law to include non-financial sectors and virtual asset service providers. Secondly, it strengthens identification for beneficial owners so that legal persons don't serve to conceal illicit funds. Third, it establishes mechanisms to apply without delay targeted financial sanctions and asset freezes required by UN Security Council resolutions. Fourth, it establishes a national coordination body between the oversight, financial intelligence, investigation, and criminal prosecution authorities. Through this act, Guatemala is aligning its legal order with the recommendations of the Financial Action Task Force. In addition, we are complying with the obligations under the International Convention for the Suppression of the Financing of Terrorism and Resolution 1373 of the Security Council. This project has been complemented by the recent adoption of legislation to combat criminal groups and transnational terrorist criminal organizations called maras or gangs. Guatemala recalls that peace and security are mainly achieved through education, decent work, and opportunities for young people. Guatemala will continue to work and to join forces to build a more resilient nation. Finally, Guatemala takes this opportunity to express its thanks for the support of the United Nations Office on Counter-Terrorism and other partners in this collective endeavor. Thank you very much.
I thank the distinguished representative of Guatemala for the statement. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Israel.

Thank you, Madam Chair. Allow me first to congratulate you and the members of the Bureau on your election and offer Israel's commitment to you in the 81st session of the Sixth Committee. Madam Chair, in June 2026, The General Assembly endorsed by vast majority the ninth review of the UN Global Counterterrorism Strategy, which while sounding like a great achievement, essentially performed technical rollover of the eighth review of the GCTS endorsed in 2023. We believe that this lengthy, repetitive, and insufficient document neglected the recent massive shifts in terrorism capabilities in the recent years. On October 7th, 2023, the world received a stunning example of the gap between the theory reflected in UN document and the reality of the terrorist threat. Counterterrorism should have evolved to meet this evolving threat. Terrorist groups continue to innovate using emerging technologies and novel methods to exploit holes in global security networks. Terrorists find methods of financing that are increasingly difficult to trace and incite and recruit lone wolf potential operatives online. They take advantage of loopholes in international law, abuse immunities and inavailability of UN premises, and convert UN infrastructure into safe havens of terror. And yet, while the terrorists sprint to the finish line, the world has dropped out of the race. Madam Chair. Israel reaffirms its unwavering commitment to the eliminating terrorism around the globe. In the face of this ongoing threat, it is critical that the world comes together to confront and destroy the spread of terrorism in all its forms and manifestations. In the face of this ongoing threat, it is critical that the world comes together to confront and destroy the spread of terrorism in all its forms and manifestations. Madam Chair, Israel is closely familiar with the agony of terrorism. Terrorism and its tragic consequences hang over us like a shadow, and the ghost of our pain haunt us without end. Today, according to the Jewish calendar, we mark the third national remembrance day of the October 7th massacre. It is no coincidence that I chose to wear the yellow ribbon pin today, the symbol we wore as our hostages were held in the tunnel tunnels of Gaza while we fought for their immediate and unconditional release. Today, even with all of our hostages, the living and the dead, finally home, this yellow ribbon pin remains a stark reminder that the suffering caused by terrorism does not simply end. It leaves scars on the victims, the survivors, and their families, and on the entire society, both in body and soul. These scars remain through the long road to recovery. so too does the pain of the families of the victims who will never see their loved ones again. At the same time, there is no sole ownership of suffering and pain. We mourn, as anyone must, the death of any innocent civilians without exception. On the other hand, the terrorist groups Hamas, Hezbollah, and other Iranian proxies intentionally sacrifice their own people, embedding themselves within densely populated areas and using their civilians as human shields. Madam Chair, Israel has faced the worst of the worst and is more determined than ever to eradicate the threat of terrorism. We must unite to cut off terrorism financing, illicit shipment of weapons, and all other forms of inducement of terrorism. We must also prevent and penalize all support for terrorism. We must shut down highly effective terrorist recruitment indoctrination efforts carried out through social media, education system, and religious institutions. We must make clear that children are not tools of warfare, and we must protect them from being indoctrinated into evil terrorist agendas. Madam Chair, we recently marked the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 devastating terror attack on this very city. In its aftermath, the UN came together to pass Security Council Resolution 1373 in 2001, laying the groundwork for the international designation and persecution of terrorist organizations. It was a moment that the world came together and decided with one voice that terrorism would not be tolerated, no matter where or whom it affected. But that was 2001. Just last week, on the 30th of September, in an act of terror, a pilot on a commercial flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv attempted to crash the aircraft with its passengers on board. The potential catastrophe was averted through the extraordinary courage and swift actions of the Israeli passengers on the aircraft and the injured captain. Their actions prevented what could have been another mass casualty terrorist attack against dozens of Israeli innocent civilians. The fact that this terror attack failed does not mean that we can discount the great threat to peace and security that it represents. Madam Chair, this time our citizen made it home safe, however, Three years ago, we were not as fortunate. This week marks the third anniversary of the October 7th massacre, the deadliest slaughter of Jews since the Holocaust. And yet, the United Nations still has not designated Hamas, Hezbollah, or the Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps as terrorist organizations. Even in this room, there are still those who have refused to unequivocally condemn these atrocities. Madam Chair, the Iranian terror regime and its proxies spread terror on the world, exporting destructions and fear to surrounding countries in the region. They have made it crystal clear that if given the opportunity, they will repeat October 7th massacre again and again until the annihilation of the state of Israel. We will not allow this to happen. We warned for years about Hamas atrocities infiltrating to the rents of UNRWA, about the global reach of the Iranian terror regime, and about the danger of the Jewish lives posed by the normalization of anti-Semitic rhetoric. Tragically, we were met with deafening silence. Madam Chair, the silence has consequences. We are witnessing a rise of antisemitism that the like of which we have not seen in nearly a century. This dangerous phenomenon is serving as a trigger for antisemitic terrorism worldwide, whether in Bondi Beach, Australia, on Hanukkah, outside the Jewish Museum in Washington, D.C., or at a synagogue in London or Canada on Yom Kippur. Madam Chair, the price of terrorism is not abstract. In Israel, it has face. Today, all of our surviving hostages taken by Hamas on October 7th are home, coping with deep, permanent scars of both their bodies and souls. They are trying to rebuild their broken lives, yet some of our hostages did not make it home alive. They joined the thousands of Israelis who have been murdered in terrorist attacks since our state's establishment. Their sacrifice will remain with us always, a solemn reminder of the danger that lurks on our borders. Madam Chair, we will not give up. We remain committed to diplomacy and collaboration and are ready and willing to work with whoever will come to the table. But make no mistake, we will never compromise the security of the State of Israel and its people. We will rise about any challenge that comes to our way and we will prevail. Thank you, Madam Chair.
I thank the distinguished representative of Israel for the statement, and I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of China.

We stand ready to work with.

You, the other members of the Bureau, and all delegations to ensure the success of the Committee's work. This year, the law on promoting ethnic unity and progress was enacted and implemented. further strengthening the legal framework for ethnic unity and social stability. Chair. China stands ready to continue working with all parties, guided by the vision of a community with a shared future for mankind, to implement the Global Security Initiative and the Global Governance Initiative, jointly advance the international counterterrorism cause, combat terrorism in all its forms and manifestations, and make active efforts towards building a world of lasting peace and universal security. They cannot respond to transnational threats through scale or coercive power alone. Their security depends on international cooperation, effective international institutions, timely information sharing, and technical expertise, and rules that apply equally to all. Counterterrorism measures must be fully consistent with the UN Charter and international law. Greater clarity in international legal framework can help reduce ambiguity, strengthen cooperation, and ensure that counterterrorism efforts are not undermined by selective interpretations of international law. The Moldovans believe that our collective response must ultimately strengthen both security and sovereignty. does international cooperation leave every state, including the smallest, better able to protect its people and preserve its freedom to shape its future? I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Maldives for the statement, and I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of the Syrian Arab Republic.

Syria The new Syria, having inherited a heavy legacy of authoritarianism and terrorism, is moving forward with restoring security and rebuilding its national institutions. Madam Chair, allow me to congratulate the Chair and the other members of the Bureau on your election and to assure you of Brazil's constructive engagement in the work ahead. The question has been before the General Assembly since its 27th session. Since 1963, states have adopted 19 international legal instruments to prevent terrorist acts, to which the General Assembly and the Security Council have added a vast body of resolutions. These documents provide us with key parameters that allow us to distinguish international terrorism from other phenomena, such as transnational organized crime. This distinction is not merely a matter of semantics. The success of international cooperation against these challenges, to which Brazil is unequivocally committed, depends on accurate legal notions and appropriate measures to tackle them. There is no basis for an automatic association between these two concepts. just as there is no basis for automatically equating transnational criminality with threats to international peace and security. Our common challenges are significant, and they demand coherent, effective, and adequate international cooperation. Naturally, this applies also to this scourge of terrorism. That is why Brazil has advocated for a comprehensive convention on international terrorism, one that may serve as a clear, stable, and reliable framework for collective action. Domestic legislation have produced a multitude of divergent definitions and punitive measures, leaving us poorly coordinated against a threat that is frequently transnational. Successive United Nations special rapporteurs have repeatedly voiced concern over domestic definitions of terrorism that are too broad and too imprecise. The label of terrorism must never become an instrument for political ends. be it as a means to silence legitimate internal opposition or to isolate states that do not in fact promote terrorism. Nor should it serve as a justification to inflict collective punishment on civilian populations in flagrant breach of international humanitarian law. Allegations of terrorism must never be used as excuses for the unilateral use of force against the territorial integrity or political independence of any state. much less for violations of human rights law and international humanitarian law. Furthermore, we cannot forget that eliminating terrorism goes beyond merely preventing and punishing terrorist acts. We must also address its root causes. The global counterterrorism strategy recognizes conditions that are conducive to terrorism, while stressing that none of them can justify it. Let us not postpone again the convening of a high-level conference under the auspices of the UN to conclude this convention. Let us translate our unanimous condemnation of terrorism into the means to efficiently combat it. We have a common duty before us. Let us fulfill it with diligence and urgency. I thank you.

My country believes that Implementing effective measures to counter terrorism takes legal certainty as to what constitutes terrorism. Therefore, Mexico reiterates the importance of moving forward with the work aimed at concluding a comprehensive convention on international terrorism, based on a clear definition that is compatible with international law and the purposes of the Charter. This would help to harmonize the international response and prevent selective application that hampers cooperation among states. In this regard, we must preserve the legal distinction between terrorism and transnational organized crime. While both phenomena may involve violence or make use of illicit networks, Their purposes and applicable legal frameworks are not interchangeable. Transnational organized crime is committed for financial or material benefit, whereas terrorism seeks to create a state of terror. Conflating the two can lead to flawed assessments, ineffective strategies, stigmatization, and the undue application of exceptional measures. In this regard, we draw attention to the analysis published on 20 September by the UN Special Rapporteur on the promotion and protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms while countering terrorism, Mr. Ben Saul, who emphasizes this legal distinction. Madam Chair. Mexico is convinced that terrorism cannot be eradicated solely through military or security responses. Violence only breeds more violence. Strategies centered on the use of force can exacerbate conflicts, increase the suffering of civilian populations, and fuel new forms of radicalization. While such measures may at times be necessary, We must not forget that this phenomenon can be addressed on a number of fronts, one of which is prevention. Our approach must be geared towards combating terrorism today and preventing its further growth and proliferation into the future. Prevention means addressing the structural conditions that facilitate recruitment and the spread of extremist narratives. In this context, a gender perspective plays a crucial role. It is not enough to recognize the differentiated impact of terrorism on women, girls and adolescents. We should also examine the impact of gender stereotypes and the models of masculinity associated with domination, aggression and the violent resolution of conflicts, which could be exploited to strengthen terrorism. Conversely, the promotion of positive masculinities, substantive equality and the effective participation of women contributes to preventing violence and strengthening communities. All measures to counter terrorism must fully respect international law, including international human rights law and international humanitarian law. The protections and safeguards afforded under those bodies of law are grounded in fundamental considerations of humanity that States must uphold. Mexico will continue to promote a multilateral, preventive and legal response, one that seeks to address the root causes of terrorism and effectively combat it. We invite other States to share this approach with us. Thank you.

After decades of discussions, pending issues remain.
