A comprehensive, widely accepted convention would strengthen the international legal framework and cooperation among States to prevent, investigate and punish terrorism in accordance with international law. Due to its transnational nature, this threat demands coordinated responses that adapt to the emerging risks, with full respect for human rights and the principles and purposes of the United Nations Charter. Panama will continue to work with all delegations to advance towards a comprehensive convention that strengthens international cooperation and enables a concerted response to terrorism. Thank you very much.
I thank the Permanent Representative of Panama for that statement, and I now give the floor to the Distinguished Representative of Yemen. You have the floor.

Thank you, Madam Chair. At the outset, allow me to congratulate you on Your election at the helm of the Sixth Committee, we wish you and members of the Bureau every success. The Republic of Yemen reiterates its steadfast rejection of terrorism and extremism in all their forms, manifestations, and sources. Terrorism should not be linked to any religion, nationality, civilization, or ethnic group. We commit to undertaking all necessary measures to combat this scourge that threatens international peace and security, undermines development and stability. The Republic of Yemen faces a growing threat posed by the terrorist Houthi militias. This threat is no longer confined to our borders, but menaces the region and the international community as a whole. The support provided to the militia by the Iranian regime strengthened its military capabilities, including maritime and missile capabilities. They are now increasingly capable of using drones and exploiting emerging technologies to pose a threat to regional and international stability and security. We stress the need for the international community to ensure the effective and full implementation of relevant Security Council resolutions, including 2216. We stress the need of undertaking all necessary measures to prevent access to military technology and weapons to sanctioned terrorist groups. We stress in this regard that threats to international maritime navigation constitutes a threat to international peace and security. Protecting waterways requires strengthening the capabilities of our state institutions, including our coast guard, as well as the dismantlement of transnational organized crime and smuggling networks. The latest escalation by the Houthi militias is not confined to humanitarian consequences within our country. It is a part of the strategic scheme to impose a new military order by the Houthi militias and their Iranian sponsor. This reveals the transnational threat posed by the Houthi militias as they seek to expand this confrontation and threaten the security of neighboring countries. This serves regional escalation and jeopardizes the security and stability of the region, as well as the interests of neighboring countries. We strongly condemn the terrorist attacks waged by the terrorist Houthi militias against the KSA, including attempts to target Mecca through drones, in addition to attacks against vital infrastructure of Al-Masjid an-Nabawi in Medina. This constitutes a blatant violation of the sovereignty of the KSA and the inviolability of its holy sites. They are a threat to the security of civilians and a deliberate provocation of the sentiments of dozens of millions or of hundreds of millions of Muslims across the world. Madam Chair, combating terrorism is a collective responsibility that requires international cooperation to strengthen the capabilities by conflict-affected countries This also requires the strengthening of their counterterrorism institutions. We reiterate the importance of the role of the UNCT in providing technical assistance and capacity building for member states. We call for strengthened programs to assist Yemen, including to dry up the funding for terrorism, as well as information sharing and cooperation frameworks to support our state institutions to dismantle networks that provide financing to terrorist groups, including the Houthi militias. This, in turn, can bolster security and stability in Yemen and the region. I thank you, Madam Chair.

I thank the distinguished.

Delegate of Yemen for that intervention. And I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Singapore. You have the floor, Madam.

Madam Vice-Chair, Singapore congratulates Ambassador Trishala Pussod, you and members of the Bureau on your election. I assure you of Singapore's full support during the session. We align ourselves with the statement made by NAM and ASEAN. We also wish to thank the Secretary-General for his report. Madam Vice-Chair, terrorism remains a serious threat to international peace and security. The global terrorism landscape is constantly evolving. It continues to present novel challenges that require the collective effort of the international community at the domestic, regional and international levels to overcome. Singapore has taken measures to counter terrorism at all three levels. First, Singapore's 2026 Terrorism Threat Assessment Report assessed that the terrorism threat to Singapore remains high. In particular, the threat of self-radicalisation including among youths exposed to extremist content online, is a serious concern. The report underscores the importance of identifying and reporting early signs of radicalisation and suspicious activities, and encourages members of the public to play an active role in safeguarding Singapore. Public vigilance is therefore a critical part of our response. We also remain committed to disrupting the financing that enables terrorism. We periodically update our National Strategy for Countering the Financing of Terrorism and the Terrorism Financing National Risk Assessment, which reflect our continued efforts to countering terrorism financing threats and maintaining a robust and updated framework. Second, at the regional level, Singapore is engaged in the war against terrorism through various ASEAN initiatives, which have been elaborated by the Distinguished Representative of Cambodia on behalf of ASEAN. The cross-sectoral coordination to address the multifaceted aspects of terrorism and violent extremism is done through the ASEAN Plan of Action to Prevent and Counter the Rise of Radicalisation and Violent Extremism. Third, Singapore remains committed to the global fight against international terrorism. We are party to 15 international counter-terrorism agreements, and continue to firmly support the UN Global Counter-Terrorism Strategy as it enters its 20th anniversary of adoption. We appreciate the ongoing efforts of the General Assembly to regularly implement and update the Strategy, including the ninth review of the Strategy which was recently concluded. Singapore also hosts the Counter-Terrorism Information Facility, which works closely with partner countries to enhance information exchange at the operational level to combat transnational terrorism and strengthen regional peace and security. Madam Vice-Chair, the General Assembly has established a working group with a view to finalising the process on the draft comprehensive convention on international terrorism, as well as discussions on convening a high-level conference under the auspices of the UN. My delegation looks forward to working closely with this working group as part of our collective efforts to achieve consensus on these matters. I thank you.
I thank the Minister of Singapore for that intervention. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Uganda. You have the floor, sir.

Madam Chair, I have the honour to deliver this statement on behalf of the delegation of the Republic of Uganda. At the outset, please allow me to congratulate you and other members of the Bureau on your election to steer the work of the Sixth Committee. It is particularly gratifying to see you up there guiding our work this afternoon. Godspeed. My delegation aligns itself with the statements made on behalf of the African Group the Organization of the Islamic Cooperation, OIC, and the Non-Aligned Movement, NAM. Uganda would like to express its gratitude to the Secretary-General for his report on measures to eliminate international terrorism, contained in document A/81/218. Madam Chair, Uganda condemns terrorism in all its forms and manifestations, for whatever purpose and by whomsoever. Terrorism can never be justified under any pretext. We reiterate our position that in order to have a meaningful, successful fight against terrorism, we must be prepared to take the hard decisions, including assigning a comprehensive definition of terrorism. This is a minimum requirement that isolates terrorism and thus differentiating it from other legitimate struggles. Terrorist acts constitutes one of the most flagrant violations of international law, including international humanitarian and human rights law. in particular, the right to life, leading to the lack of full enjoyment of human rights and fundamental freedoms of peoples. And that such acts endanger the territorial integrity and stability of states, as well as nationals, regional and international security, destabilize legitimately constituted governments or the prevailing constitutional order and political unity of states that affect the stability of nations and the very basis of societies, as well as create adverse consequences on the economic and social development and cause the destruction of the physical and economic infrastructure of states. Madam Chair, the circumstances and conditions under which terrorism thrives must be addressed before there can be any hope to ultimately eradicate the threat. In order to eradicate the problem, the root causes must be identified. Accordingly, poverty must be addressed as one of the conditions under which terrorism thrives. terrorism cannot and should not be associated with any religion, nationality, civilization, or ethnic group, and that these attributions should not be used to justify terrorism or counter-terrorism measures that include, in particular, profiling of terror suspects and intrusion on individual privacy. My delegation fully appreciates and supports the work done so far by the Ad Hoc Committee in drafting a comprehensive convention in international terrorism. We reiterate the importance of the inclusion of a comprehensive convention of combating international terrorism and the continued effort to that end. We welcome the resumption of the informal consultations on the outstanding issues relating to the draft CCIT, and we further call upon Member States to cooperate in resolving the outstanding issues. My delegation stands ready to work actively with other delegations to achieve consensus regarding the draft comprehensive convention on international terrorism. My delegation supports the establishment of the United Nations Programme Office for Counter-Terrorism and Training in Africa, which will make an important contribution in counter-terrorism through capacity building support to Member States of the region. It will serve as a training hub to build counter-terrorism capacities and cooperation in Africa, particularly in West Africa and the Sahel. This training hub will develop and deliver specialized counterterrorism and law enforcement training programs to requesting member states in Africa. My delegation also welcomes the establishment of a regional program office of counterterrorism in Nairobi, Kenya, to prevent and counter violent extremism conducive to terrorism in East Africa. Madam Chair, we must collectively engage in efforts aimed at denying terrorists any havens, eradicating such sources of terrorist financing, reducing state vulnerability, and enhancing emergency preparedness and response capabilities. Under the auspices of the African Union, Uganda is the biggest contributor to the AUSSOM forces, and in that capacity, Uganda has been at the forefront of fighting terrorist groups. In some situations, terrorists take advantage of weak government structures in order to force recruits into their ranks. We welcome the adoption by consensus of the General Assembly resolution 78/43, entitled "Measures to prevent terrorist from acquiring weapons of mass destruction. It is stressed that the most effective way of preventing terrorists from acquiring weapons of mass destruction is through the elimination of such weapons at all. Madam Chair, Uganda remains resolute in its commitment to combat terrorism through adherence to international legal instruments, aligning our national strategies with global counterterrorism to ensure a comprehensive approach to security and public safety. Uganda is at the forefront of implementing these instruments to counter the menace effectively. We value and support the technical assistance provided by UNODC as highlighted in resolution 78/226 and 79/229, which are pivotal in enhancing our national capacities to tackle terrorism-related challenges. Addressing these challenges and obstacles requires a multifaceted approach that involves strengthening institutional capacities enhancing transparency and accountability mechanisms, and fostering partnerships with civil society organizations, and raising awareness about legal rights among the general population. Further, there is need to ensure that international frameworks and legislative bodies adapt swiftly to rapid advancements in technology, ensuring legal frameworks which can promptly identify and address emerging challenges by: a) putting in place structures for proactive measures to fight crime, to facilitate research and inform the emerging trends in the criminal justice system; b) encouraging joint investigations and prosecution, not necessarily by States affected by terrorism at a given time, but by means by teams to observe, document, and make recommendations for future use. C, reviewing mechanisms for success stories. For example, Uganda and the world over had and still have many lessons to learn and unlearn from the 2010 bombing case that is key to the investigation and prosecution of terrorism. D, clarifying on the issue of costs of mutual legal assistance. This should be given more clarity in international cooperation, if international cooperation is to be realized. Many international instruments leave it to the requested country, but this should not be if reasonable cost is to be realized. Reasonability is left to individual interpretation, which makes it even more complicated to practically comprehend and implement. And e, acknowledging that technology advancement is at different levels in different member states. This affects the ability to respond to requests that are beyond a state's technological capacity. In conclusion, Madam Chair, Uganda reaffirms its commitment to promoting international cooperation and technical assistance in preventing terrorism and other forms of transboundary crime. By working together with the global community, Uganda aims at strengthening its law enforcement capacities, enhance international cooperation, and combating terrorism effectively. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Uganda for that statement, and I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Indonesia. You have the floor, sir.

Thank you, Madam Chair. Allow me to begin by congratulating the Chair and members of the Bureau on their elections and thanking the Secretary General for his report on these agenda items. We align ourselves with the statement delivered by Cambodia, Iran, and Saudi Arabia on behalf of ASEAN, the Non-Aligned Movement, and the OIC, respectively. 20 years after the global counterterrorism strategy was adopted, the threat has changed. Terrorist networks are more decentralized, driven by small cells and lone actors. They exploit new technologies, fund themselves through crimes, and feed on unresolved conflict and hatred. Yet as the threat evolves, our unity has frayed. This year's review of the strategy broke a 20-year tradition of consensus. Against this backdrop, allow me to highlight three reflections. First, prevention that puts people at the center. Security measures alone cannot defeat terrorism. Indonesia continues to champion a whole of government and the whole of society effort. In February this year, we adopted our new national action plan on preventing and countering violent extremism for 2026 to 2029. The national plan underlined the important role of families, communities, schools, religious leaders, and civil society. It is guided by human rights, gender equality, and child protections. In practice, this means children recruited by terrorist group are treated first as victims. A principal Indonesia advanced through ECOSOC resolution 2024/12. Second, confronting terrorism in the digital age. Last year, more than 100 Indonesian children were exposed to radicalizations through online games and social media. Some were drawn not by ideology, but by online communities glorifying violence. In response, we are removing harmful content and requiring platforms to verify users' age and provide reporting channels for children. But beyond recruitment, terrorist groups increasingly exploit the digital space to move illicit funds. Responding to this, as the Secretary-General's report shows, states are tightening asset-freezing rules and closing new channels such as crypto assets. Indonesia has also done its part. Our legal regime ensures that the assets of designated terrorists are frozen without delay, while ensuring access to legal remedies. Third, strengthening international cooperation. Terrorism knows no borders, and our closest neighbors are our immediate partners. Building on the ASEAN Convention on Counter-Terrorism, Indonesia initiated the Bali Work Plan, bringing 19 ASEAN bodies together on prevention. Last year, ASEAN leaders adopted the declarations on the use of sports for preventing violent extremism, emphasizing the role of sport in building tolerance and social inclusion. Earlier this year, with Malaysia and Philippines, and with the United Nations support, Indonesia completed the first regional study of young gamers' exposures to violent extremist content. Youth from our three countries are actively contributing to shape the policies meant to protect them. Madam Chair, acts of terrorism are unjustifiable in any circumstances and must never be associated with any religion, nationality, civilizations, or ethnic group. 20 years ago, we agreed on common strategy. Two years ago, in Pact for the Future, we resolved to build a future free from terrorism. The threat will keep changing. Our resolve must not. Indonesia stands ready to do its part at home, with our neighbors, and together with all of you. I thank you, Madam Chair.
I thank the distinguished representative of Indonesia for that statement and now give the floor to the distinguished delegate of Uruguay. You have the floor, Madam.

Thank you very much, Madam Vice-Chair. Since this is the first time my delegation is taking the floor, allow me to congratulate you and other members of the Bureau on your election, and we wish you every success in your role. At this time, we would like to take the floor in our national capacity to complement the statement that we made on behalf of the Community of Latin American and Caribbean States, CELAC. Madam Vice-Chair, Uruguay roundly condemns terrorism in all of its forms and manifestations and reaffirms its commitment to prevent and combat it strictly in compliance with the UN Charter and international law, including international human rights law, international refugee law and international humanitarian law. Our country believes that an effective response to terrorism requires strengthened international cooperation, with the UN playing a central role based on respect for the rule of law and the international resolutions. This year sees the ninth review of the UN Global Counter-Terrorism Strategy on the 20th anniversary of its adoption. We supported the resolution that was adopted as since the strategy is a common framework to strengthen the efforts of the international community in combating terrorism. At the same time, we regret the fact that for the first time since adoption in 2006, a review of the strategy was not able to reach consensus and it had to be put to a vote. We also believe that the outcome of the ninth review didn't fully reflect the level of ambition that the current circumstances require. We hope that this experience will allow us to learn lessons for future reviews and to recover the spirit of consensus that traditionally characterizes this process. Without prejudice to this, Uruguay particularly values the fact that we have maintained a clear distinction between terrorism and transnational organized crime. While there could be links between both phenomena, we believe that it is fundamental to avoid equating them with each other with interchangeable formulations. These are distinct phenomena that need responses that are tailored to the applicable legal frameworks. We also reiterate the need to combat the financing of terrorism and prevent those who are committing or supporting acts of terrorism using material, logistical or financial resources. At a national level, we reiterate that we continue to strengthen our institutional and legal framework. This We are implementing our national strategy on money laundering, the financing of terrorism and the spread of weapons of mass destruction, as well as the plan of action which was adopted in 2025 through the relevant decree, which establishes the lines of action to be carried out until 2030. Uruguay also maintains close cooperation with the counterterrorism strategy of the UN Security Council and the Executive Directorate. In the visits carried out to our country, we have had constructive dialogue with the CTED on pending challenges, the achievements and their implementation, their recommendations. We value this cooperation mechanism, which contributes to strengthening, building national capacities and identifying priority areas for technical Furthermore, our country is implementing the relevant resolutions of the Security Council in terrorism and applies the relevant measures on the basis of consolidated lists. Madam Vice-Chair, to conclude, Uruguay reaffirms its commitment to continue working constructively at a bilateral, regional and international level with all States to strengthen international cooperation against terrorism, preserving the central role of the UN. Thank you very much.
